newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan lowers domestic coal prices to utilities.
newsitem.headline: Japan lowers domestic coal prices to utilities.

text.p: In a bid to ease the burden placed upon power utilities in Japan's latest push for lower electricity rates, the government has lowered the standard price utilities must pay for domestic coal.
Prices were lowered by 1,000 yen to roughly 16,500 yen per tonne, according to the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).

As part of a government policy aimed at protecting Japan's ailing coal industry, power utilities have been forced to pay nearly three times the price of imports for domestic coal and purchase nearly all of the supplies domestic mines produce.
Government pressure to lower electricity rates paid by consumers to more representative international levels led the power utility industry to issue a formal request that coal prices be lowered.
MITI officials said coal prices vary regionally depending on transportation costs.
Before the coal price cuts, the lowest price, paid by customers in Hokkaido, was 17,057 yen per tonne, while customers in central Japan's Chubu region paid the highest rate of 19,336 yen per tonne.
Japan coal mining, a once-powerful industry which helped fuel Japan's massive industrial base, has been made increasingly obsolescent by cheaper regional imports.
In March, Japan's largest and oldest coal mine, Mitsui Coal Mining Co Ltd's Miike mine in Fukuoka prefecture, southern Japan, was shut down. Nearly 2,000 people were laid off.
The two mines remaining -- on the northern island of Hokkaido and southern prefecture of Nagasaki -- are likely to meet the same fate when government subsidies dry up in 2002, analysts said.
